title: Posthumous Likeness Trusts for Creators
one_liner: Estate planning for people whose face and voice already earn money: who may license their AI replica, who may not, and how it is enforced.
customer: Mid-tier creators (100K-5M followers), podcasters, voice actors, and the small managers and MCNs who represent them.
problem: Consumer-grade video and voice cloning means anyone's likeness can be recreated after death. Laws are a patchwork (Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's 2024 digital-replica laws, a federal NO FAKES bill pending). Creators' estates hold real income (channels, catalogs, sponsorships) but have no instrument to permit, forbid or license replicas. Platforms handle it ad hoc.
solution: A 'Likeness Trust Kit': (1) a will or trust addendum with a digital-replica directive (allowed uses, revenue splits, ban list, who decides), (2) a registry and notice system aimed at platforms and AI vendors, (3) monitoring for unauthorized replicas and template takedowns, (4) a channel-continuity plan (access, memorialization, pinned messages), and (5) an optional licensing desk for approved 'legacy' uses.
why_now: The fall-2025 backlash over AI videos of deceased public figures made estates' concerns public. State post-mortem publicity laws changed in 2024, and platforms have begun shipping likeness-detection tools for creators (verify current status). No estate product has priced in that a voice and face are now licensable and misusable assets.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,500 setup for documents and registry, $19-$79/month monitoring, and 10-20% of licensed uses. Managers buy in bulk.
non_obvious_insight: Estate lawyers treat likeness as a celebrity issue. The willing buyers are working creators who already understand platforms and already earn from their persona, and they are numerous and reachable through managers.
first_30_days: Partner with an entertainment attorney. Draft a template addendum. Sell to 10 creator managers at about $2K per client. Use off-the-shelf detection tools for monitoring and publish a public 'creator death checklist' for lead generation.

title: Burn-Lot Exit Desk for Fire Survivors
one_liner: Package burned lots and stranded insurance claims into sellable assets, and auction them to vetted builders at fair prices.
customer: Owners of destroyed lots in the Palisades and Altadena (free to them). Builders, small developers and community land trusts pay a success fee.
problem: About 13% of affected Palisades single-family owners have started rebuilding 18-plus months on. Insurer estimates ($462/sq ft) sit far below contractor budgets (up to $1,065). Many owners do not want to become developers, and cash buyers lowball lots.
solution: Prepare each lot as a marketable asset: claim documents (what transfers and what does not), debris and utility status, pre-approved plans and permit history. Run a competitive bid among vetted builders with three options: sell the lot, sell with claim assignment, or take a fixed-price turnkey rebuild. Handle escrow and title through partners.
why_now: Deadlines on additional-living-expense coverage and permit pipelines are biting 18 months after the fires, and the low rebuild rate shows demand for an exit.
revenue_model: A 2-3% buyer-paid success fee, builder subscriptions for deal flow, and later turnkey rebuild margin.
non_obvious_insight: 'Rebuilding services' is the obvious market. The larger one is liquidity: turning a lot plus a claim into cash at a fair price.
first_30_days: Interview 30 owners in fire-survivor groups, recruit 3 builders, and hand-run 5 lots. Use a licensed broker partner for the transaction side.

title: Translator-Owned Language Trusts for Public Services
one_liner: Translator co-ops that build and license verified medical, legal, and benefits corpora for refugee and diaspora languages, and sell certified human review to agencies that now rely on machine translation.
customer: State Medicaid and benefits agencies, hospital systems, courts, and school districts serving speakers of Karen, Somali, Kirundi, Tigrinya, Haitian Creole, Hmong, Dari, and similar languages. Agencies pay per-word review and $50-150k annual contracts. AI labs and voice-AI vendors license evaluation and fine-tuning data.
problem: General translation is commoditized, so translators are displaced. But in low-resource languages, machine translation of consent forms, discharge instructions, and benefits notices is wrong in dangerous ways, and agencies use it because human capacity has evaporated. Translators' glossaries and corrections are given away or locked in agency-owned translation memories, and gig data platforms pay a pittance.
solution: A member-owned trust per language cluster. Translators contribute and verify domain glossaries and parallel corpora under community governance with consent, revenue share, and veto rights. The trust sells (a) certified human review of machine-translated public-service documents with a warranty, (b) benchmarks and licensed data to vendors, with usage royalties passed to members, and (c) an MT-plus-human-guardrails workflow for agencies.
why_now: The HHS Section 1557 rule (2024) requires qualified human review when machine translation is used on critical health documents, and it remains in effect in 2026, which creates non-discretionary demand. The Mozilla Data Collective opened paid commercial licensing of community datasets and the Gates Foundation has committed to language AI. Freelance translation rates have collapsed.
revenue_model: Per-word certified-review fees, annual agency retainers, data and benchmark licenses, and patronage dividends to member translators.
non_obvious_insight: A translator's most valuable asset is not their time but their error corrections in narrow domains, which is precisely what every model is worst at. The co-op structure solves both community trust and individual freelancers' lack of bargaining power, and legal language-access duties turn the buyer's budget from discretionary to mandatory.
first_30_days: Pick one language and one metro with a large diaspora, such as Karen speakers in St. Paul. Recruit 10-15 translators as founding members. Offer a hospital system or county health department a paid pilot to review its top 50 patient documents against Section 1557 requirements. Build the glossary in shared tooling and sign a governance charter.

title: Crash-Test Ratings for Collusive Pricing Agents
one_liner: A simulation lab and clean-room negotiation venue that certifies your pricing or negotiating agent does not tacitly collude with counterpart agents, like Euro NCAP for antitrust.
customer: General counsel, antitrust counsel and pricing or procurement heads at companies deploying pricing or negotiation agents: property managers and landlords, hotels, insurers, freight brokers, ad-buying agencies and retailers. Pricing-software vendors who are being sued are the first buyers.
problem: Two LLM agents that repeatedly interact can converge on supracompetitive prices with no human ever agreeing to anything. The law is moving fast: California's AB 325 took effect January 1, 2026, the DOJ RealPage settlement landed in late 2025, and DOJ officials said in May 2026 that 'software cannot launder collusion'. Deployers have no way to show their agent is clean.
solution: A harness that plays your agent against a zoo of counterpart agents (clones of itself, competitor-like agents, vendor agents) across thousands of repeated-game scenarios. It measures price convergence, punishment and signaling patterns, and information leakage, and issues a rated report plus CI regression tests. A hosted clean-room negotiation venue firewalls competitors' inputs and keeps regulator-readable logs. Partner economists and an antitrust firm sign the report.
why_now: AB 325 and its lowered pleading standard, active DOJ and state enforcement, private class actions over pricing algorithms, and agent-to-agent negotiation going live with the 2026 commerce protocols. Academic work has shown LLM pricing agents can settle on collusive outcomes without instruction.
revenue_model: $25-150k per audit, $2-5k per month for CI-integrated monitoring, and expert-witness and defense-support add-ons revenue-shared with partner economists.
non_obvious_insight: The exculpatory evidence is counterfactual behavior: what your agent would do if a rival raised its price. Only the deployer can generate that evidence, and it is cheap to produce in simulation, so antitrust compliance can be turned into unit tests. Because plausible-agreement pleading is now enough to survive dismissal, having a dated, third-party test record is worth far more than its price.
first_30_days: Team up an industrial-organization economist and an antitrust lawyer. Publish an open 'collusion eval' benchmark of LLM repeated pricing games to build credibility. Pitch 10 rental-pricing, hospitality and freight-pricing software vendors a $25k fixed-fee 'pre-litigation' audit and close the first two within about 60 days.

title: Responsible-Charge Network for AI-Made Professional Work
one_liner: Licensed engineers and architects take legal responsibility for AI-generated permit sets per review, with a review-telemetry audit trail that also lowers malpractice premiums.
customer: AI-native firms that generate permit drawings, structural letters and MEP plans for ADUs, solar, decks and prefab, and the small design firms that use them. They need licensed sign-off in many states and don't want to employ engineers everywhere.
problem: AI can draft a permit set in an hour, but only a licensed human can seal it. Startups hire engineers state by state or rely on stamp mills. Regulators and insurers fear rubber-stamping, and 'responsible charge' (the legal standard that the professional actually directed the work) is unprovable. Existing AI-drawing companies such as Spacial keep licensed engineers in-house, so smaller entrants have no good option.
solution: A vetted network of licensed professionals paid a fixed fee per stamped package, plus software that records how the review happened: time on sheet, checks completed, redlines, overrides. That log becomes the defensible 'responsible-charge' record for state boards, and it underwrites cheaper E&O coverage through an MGA partner. Start narrow with structural and engineering letters for residential ADU, deck and solar permits in three states.
why_now: AI permit-set generators are moving from demos to real volume, and the standard practice is a licensed engineer reviewing before sealing. Professional liability carriers now ask about AI use, and licensing boards are issuing AI guidance. Nobody has built the shared review-evidence layer.
revenue_model: 25% to 35% take on engineer fees of $150 to $600 per package. MGA commission on E&O premiums. SaaS fee for the telemetry and audit-trail software.
non_obvious_insight: In AI-delivered professional services, the scarce input is not intelligence but a person who can lose a license. Whoever holds verifiable proof of actual review owns the pricing of liability, which is worth more than the stamps. The product is explicitly anti-stamp-mill: it makes shallow review visible and expensive.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 semi-retired PEs across three states. Sign two AI-permit startups or ADU designers with a backlog. Run the review flow manually with screen recordings and checklists to gather telemetry. Meet one small-firm E&O broker about a pilot rider for reviewed AI work.

title: Swarf Stabilization for New US Magnet Plants
one_liner: Hazmat-grade stabilization, transport and recycler routing for the pyrophoric NdFeB grinding swarf that new US magnet plants will produce in tonnes.
customer: New and expanding US sintered-magnet makers and independent magnet grinding shops, who pay per-kg handling. Recyclers and re-melters are the downstream buyers.
problem: US magnet capacity is ramping (MP Materials broke ground on a Texas magnet campus in Feb 2026 on a DoD-backed deal). Machining and grinding turn a large share of sintered NdFeB, often 20-30%, into oil-wet, self-heating swarf and sludge. It is hard to classify, ship and store, so it drifts to overseas buyers or hazardous-waste disposal.
solution: An inerting and oil-immersion protocol, DOT-compliant packaging for self-heating solids, permitted storage through a partner, and routing to domestic recyclers or re-melters. It comes with a mass-balance certificate that lets the magnet maker claim recycled content to defense and EU customers.
why_now: Trace the chain: DoD equity and DPA-style support create new US magnet plants, which create swarf, which becomes a fire and compliance problem with no dedicated service. EU rare-earth recycled-content obligations phase in 2028-2032, and recyclers such as Cyclic Materials are funded and hunting for clean feed.
revenue_model: Handling fee per kg, plus a revenue share of recovered oxide or alloy value from recyclers, plus an annual compliance retainer.
non_obvious_insight: The near-term rare-earth urban mine is inside the factory. Swarf is clean, known-composition and available in tonnes before any end-of-life magnet wave arrives.
first_30_days: Call EHS heads at the 5 new or ramping magnet plants and 10 grinding shops. Offer a free swarf audit to quantify tonnage and value. Line up a hazmat-permitted storage and transport partner and one recycler offtake. Run a first pilot shipment.

title: Mitigation Grant Packets for Small Towns
one_liner: A packet factory and compliance tracker that gets small governments through FEMA and state mitigation grants without clawbacks.
customer: Municipalities under 25,000 people, counties, tribal governments, special districts and state emergency-management agencies, paid from management-cost lines.
problem: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order, reinstated Mar 18 2026 with $1B, and applications closed July 23 2026. Small governments lack staff for benefit-cost analysis, environmental and historic review, procurement and match documentation, and then risk clawbacks. California's new Safe Homes Grant and SB 894 revolving loan need local administration.
solution: Standardized templates for the top project types (culvert upsizing, generators, elevation, defensible space, floodproofing, safe rooms), covering benefit-cost analysis, environmental checklists and procurement. Add post-award compliance and drawdown tracking, built for several programs since BRIC timing is uncertain.
why_now: Federal funding restarted but is unstable. States are building their own programs, and big consultants ignore small jobs.
revenue_model: $6-20K fixed fee per packet and $1-2K/month compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: Government grants are gated by paperwork, and the volume of unserved demand sits in towns that big consultants skip.
first_30_days: Cold-email 200 town managers in high-hazard states with a free readiness scan, and sign 3 pilots.

title: Payroll-Deducted Paylater Refinance for Factory Workers
one_liner: Consolidate minimum-wage workers' paylater and online loans into one payroll-deducted instalment, sold to the employer as retention.
customer: Indonesian manufacturers and retailers with 1,000+ minimum-wage staff, especially in Java's industrial belts; employers pay a fee and a partner lender funds.
problem: Paylater financing reached Rp43.28T in May and online lending Rp100.69T, and defaults are rising among minimum-wage workers. Collection harassment causes absenteeism and turnover.
solution: Consolidate a worker's paylater and pinjol debts into one lower-rate loan repaid via payroll, funded by a licensed multifinance or bank partner. The wedge is three factories in Bekasi and Karawang.
why_now: OJK scrutiny is rising and the 2026 macro squeeze is pushing defaults up.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus lender spread share, and an employer fee of Rp10-15k per worker per month.
non_obvious_insight: The paylater trap is an HR problem before it is a credit problem, and the employer is the only party with payroll access and a reason to care.
first_30_days: Interview HR heads at three factories and pilot with 200 workers using a partner lender.

title: Credit Ratings and Insurance for Virtual Power Plants
one_liner: A neutral firmness rating plus a parametric shortfall policy, so hyperscalers and utilities can buy VPP megawatts they can actually count.
customer: VPP operators and installers (pay for the rating), hyperscalers and utilities buying capacity (subscribe to reports), and reinsurers and MGAs (take the risk and pay a fronting fee).
problem: Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home announced 16.8 GW of 'capacity-as-a-service' for data centers with no disclosed pricing, metering or verification standard. A 580 MW dispatch from 140k batteries on Sept 9 proves the tech works, but one event is not firm capacity. Buyers under bring-your-own-capacity rules need MW they can legally rely on.
solution: Publish a methodology that works like ELCC for distributed fleets: fleet-level P50/P90 availability by season and hour from attested device telemetry, with letter-grade tiers. Add a parametric policy, underwritten by a partner MGA or reinsurer, that pays the buyer if delivered MW falls below rated MW in a dispatch event. Start with public data from the ERCOT ADER pilot and California's DSGS program.
why_now: Hyperscaler-VPP deals, PJM's curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule and real dispatch events like Sept 9 mean there is finally enough event data to rate fleets.
revenue_model: $50-250k a year per fleet rated, subscriptions from buyers, and a fee or premium share on the insurance wrap.
non_obvious_insight: The VPP industry thinks its hard problem is enrollment. The buyer's hard problem is trust. Hyperscalers only pay for 'firm' if a third party is on the hook. Ratings plus insurance turn dispatch volatility into a financial product, and the standard-setter collects a toll on every MW sold.
first_30_days: Publish an unsolicited scorecard of public ERCOT ADER and California DSGS dispatch performance. Offer 15 VPP operators a free confidential rating in exchange for telemetry. Sound out two MGAs or reinsurers on parametric structure. Pre-sell a rating to one aggregator that is already pitching hyperscalers.

title: Pooled Buyer Mandates for Group Discounts
one_liner: Thousands of buyer agents sign standing purchase mandates ('I will pay up to $X if 200 others join') and vendors bid to fill the pooled demand.
customer: Startups and SMBs (10-200 employees) buying SaaS and business services (renewals, business insurance, telecom). Buyers pay a success fee and vendors pay for pre-committed demand.
problem: Small buyers lack bargaining power and time, and group purchasing organizations serve hospitals and enterprises, not the long tail. Vendors offer volume discounts against committed volume they cannot see. Agent payment standards now include signed intent mandates (Google's AP2, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent) that capture limits and constraints, and AP2 explicitly anticipates group scenarios, yet no product pools them.
solution: A mandate pool where each buyer or their agent signs an intent mandate with price ceiling, term and threshold. The exchange aggregates by category, shows vendors a live demand curve with reservation prices, and runs a sealed-bid reverse auction when the threshold is met. Purchases execute through each buyer's own payment mandate. First category: annual SaaS renewals, a Vendr for the long tail.
why_now: AP2 (September 2025), Verifiable Intent and UCP provide the first standard way to hold cryptographically signed, pre-authorized purchase intent. Agents now run procurement tasks, and vendors moving to agent meters want volume signals.
revenue_model: 5-10% of buyer savings or a 2-4% vendor fee on pooled transactions.
non_obvious_insight: A signed intent is a binding, machine-readable limit order for goods, so small buyers can pre-commit credibly without a human negotiating. That credibility is what makes group buying scale, like Kickstarter for procurement.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 startups from a founder community to pledge to 5 popular tools through a web form (protocol integration later). Bring the demand curve to 5 vendors and close one pooled deal to prove price.

title: Code-Cleared Church Space for Microschools
one_liner: Pair congregations with empty classroom wings and microschool or childcare operators, and sell the missing piece: pre-cleared zoning, fire and licensing paths.
customer: Microschool founders, learning-pod operators and small childcare providers who pay rent, and shrinking congregations, lodges and libraries with weekday space. Operators pay a platform fee; congregations pay for readiness passports.
problem: Microschool enrollment has grown an estimated 40% since 2023, and ESAs plus a federal scholarship tax credit starting in 2027 will add demand. Space is not the constraint; permission is. Certificate-of-occupancy, fire-marshal, egress, sprinkler and childcare-licensing rules vary by jurisdiction, so operators guess and congregations do not know what their building could legally host.
solution: For each listed building, produce a jurisdiction-specific readiness passport: occupancy class, likely deficiencies with cost estimates, pre-drawn plan sets, checklist and sequencing for approvals. Add a standard lease, child-protection policy pack and insurance bundle. Operators search by county and see how many weeks and dollars separate them from opening.
why_now: ESAs, tax-credit scholarships and state laws (Florida now lets registered microschools use former churches and similar buildings without zoning changes) are moving faster than building codes. Congregations are shrinking and buildings are costly to maintain. Treasury rulemaking on what counts as a school adds uncertainty that rewards jurisdiction-specific expertise.
revenue_model: $2k to $6k per building readiness passport, 5% of first-year rent or $250 to $500 a month platform fee from operators, insurance referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Listing space is a commodity. Pre-cleared certainty is the product, and the code-path knowledge compounds jurisdiction by jurisdiction. Each solved county becomes a reusable playbook and a barrier to competitors.
first_30_days: Pick one state that has ESAs and friendly rules (Florida, Texas, Arizona or Tennessee). Map the approval path in 3 counties. Sign 5 churches and 5 microschool operators through founder groups. Deliver the first paid passport for $3k with a code consultant.

title: Builder Defect Outbreak Radar From Permit Clusters
one_liner: Epidemiology for houses: read repair-permit clusters by builder, subdivision and vintage to tell HOA boards they have a defect outbreak and how many months remain on the legal clock.
customer: HOA management companies and reserve-study firms (about $99-250 per community per year, or a $750 one-time scan). Independent home inspectors and buyer's agents in new-build subdivisions ($19-39 per address). Later, home-warranty companies and homeowners insurers as data licensees.
problem: Production-home defects (roofs, windows, stucco or siding, plumbing, foundations) show up as patterns, but each owner sees only their own house. Boards learn late. Statutes of repose and limitation for construction-defect claims typically run roughly 6-10 years depending on state and quietly expire. Buyers pay for the defect discount without knowing why, and the MLS says nothing.
solution: Ingest city and county permit data. Use an LLM to classify messy permit text (re-roof, window replacement, siding or stucco remediation, re-pipe, foundation or pier repair, water-intrusion repair). Tie parcels to subdivision, builder and year built from plat and assessor data. Compare repair-permit rates to age-matched control cohorts in the same metro. Flag statistically significant outliers. Deliver a 'Community Defect Scan': map, cohort comparison, estimated time left under the applicable state statute (information, not legal advice), and next steps (independent engineer, reserve study update, attorney consult). Also offer a per-address flag API for inspectors.
why_now: The 2020-2022 building boom, built under labor and material shortages with substitutions, is now 4-6 years old, when defects surface and the earliest repose clocks start closing. Permit portals and open data are far more digitized than five years ago. LLMs make classification of messy permit text nearly free. Insurers and lenders are increasingly sensitive to new-build condition.
revenue_model: Community scans at $750 one-time. Management-company portfolio subscriptions at $99-250 per community per year. Per-address inspector add-on at $19-39. Data licensing to warranty and insurance underwriters. Flat fees only, with no referral fees to law firms, to avoid fee-splitting problems.
non_obvious_insight: Individual defects are invisible, but outbreaks are not. Appraisers watch this pattern for years without a feed: neighbors all re-roofing in year 5, three permits for the same water-intrusion fix on one street. The payer isn't the buyer, it's the board with a ticking legal deadline and a manager who wants to look proactive. The trick that makes a 'builder X is an outlier' claim defensible is controlling for age, since old-house repairs are normal and only age-matched cohort comparison isolates the builder.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with clean open permit data and heavy 2019-22 production building (for example Denver suburbs, Phoenix East Valley or Austin/Round Rock). Build the pipeline over about 200 subdivisions. Produce 10 free scans for community managers. Have counsel review the wording (state permit counts and method only, no accusations). Pitch 5 management companies and 3 reserve-study firms, and sell the first 10 scans at $750.

title: Exchange for Unused Grid Interconnection Headroom
one_liner: A market where owners of unused interconnection capacity and stalled queue positions sell time-sliced access to batteries and data centers that cannot wait for the queue.
customer: Sellers: owners of operating solar and wind plants whose interconnection is sized for peaks they hit only some hours a year, holders of stalled or zombie queue positions, and retiring plants holding transferable capacity rights. Buyers: battery developers, data-center developers and large electrifying industrials that need MW-scale grid access in under 24 months.
problem: Queues hold thousands of GW while data centers and storage developers wait years. Existing owners have real headroom and completed studies but no idea what they are worth or how to transfer them under FERC rules, so deals happen only through informal broker phone calls.
solution: Standardized listings: point of interconnection, headroom by hour profile (from public settlement and EIA data), completed studies and network-upgrade dollars already paid, and rule pathway (surplus interconnection service, co-location, capacity-right transfers). The platform screens deals, supports escrowed contracts and builds price discovery in $/kW-year. Later it offers time-sliced flexible contracts, for example a battery using a solar plant's line at night.
why_now: AI-driven load growth is hitting interconnection scarcity in 2026. FERC has pushed surplus and flexible interconnection, ISOs allow some capacity-right transfers, and hourly injection data makes headroom measurable for the first time.
revenue_model: 2% to 4% success fee on contract value, seller SaaS for asset managers ($1k to $3k a month for headroom analytics), and buyer-side search retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable asset is not the megawatt slot; it is the completed study and network upgrades already paid for by an earlier owner, which cut years off the timeline. Most owners do not know their headroom is worth anything.
first_30_days: Use EIA and ISO settlement data plus queue files to find 150 solar plants with low peak utilization. Cold-contact 40 asset managers, sign one exclusive listing, and take a term-sheet conversation to 15 storage and data-center developers. Target one small (about 20 MW) deal for the first success fee.

title: Outsourced Elder-Exploitation Desk for Credit Unions
one_liner: A managed service where trained specialists take flagged older-member transactions, call the member and trusted contact, file reports and document compliance.
customer: Community banks and credit unions ($300M-$5B in assets) with older memberships. Sales run through CUSOs, state leagues and core-processor marketplaces to BSA and fraud officers.
problem: Americans 60+ reported $7.7B in fraud losses in 2025 (up 59%), with an average loss over $38k and 12,400+ people losing $100k or more. Small institutions have alerts but no trained humans to call members, coordinate lawful holds, file SARs and APS reports, and prove Senior Safe Act training.
solution: Ingest the institution's flagged-alert queue and staff a desk with retired bank fraud investigators and social workers who use scripts to break the scam spell (pig-butchering, crypto-ATM, impostor). The desk coordinates holds, files APS and SAR narratives, runs annual Senior Safe Act training, and delivers quarterly avoided-loss analytics.
why_now: Investment and pig-butchering fraud is over a third of losses, older adults are adopting AI fast (23% of 65+ use ChatGPT, up from 10%), and voice-cloning scams raise stakes. State attorneys general and regulators are pressing institutions to do more.
revenue_model: $2-6k a month per institution by asset size, plus per-case fees, sold on documented avoided loss.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer fraud apps are crowded, but the institution is the party with a duty of care, and the missing capacity is human case handling, not another detection model. Pricing to avoided losses makes the ROI obvious.
first_30_days: Sell a 90-day pilot to two credit unions through a CUSO or state league, staffed by two retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Record prevented losses and hold-to-report cycle time.

title: Ratepayer Impact Statements for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, quantified 'who pays' filing for every proposed data center, like an environmental impact statement but for your electric bill.
customer: Data center developers who need a credible neutral document to win zoning or PUC approval ($50-150k per project). County governments, state consumer advocates and ratepayer coalitions ($15-40k per docket) also buy it.
problem: 7 in 10 Americans oppose data centers in their community and New York imposed a hyperscale moratorium. Residential rates are up 7.3% and utilities requested a record $31B in hikes in 2025. Nobody can credibly say how much of a specific rate case or interconnection cost a given project causes, so each side hires ad hoc experts and the fight runs on vibes.
solution: An open, auditable cost-causation model built on FERC Form 1, EIA-861, large-load tariff filings, IRP capacity plans and PJM auction results. It outputs a 10-year per-household bill delta for a specific project under different tariff terms (minimum take, collateral, bring-your-own-capacity). Deliverables are a standardized Ratepayer Impact Statement and a witness-ready exhibit. A free state-by-state 'who pays' scorecard is the top of the funnel.
why_now: Affordability is a midterm issue and opposition is now bill-driven. Utilities are adopting large-load tariffs whose terms can be modeled. Capacity prices at the cap make cost shifts visible in dollars per MWh.
revenue_model: Per-project fee from developers, per-docket fee from advocates and counties, and an annual subscription for PUC staff. Independence comes from a published fee schedule and a methodology committed in advance, as with credit rating agencies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders dismiss opposition as NIMBY, but it is really about bills, and bills are quantifiable. Whoever owns the accepted number owns the approval process. Both sides will pay for it, the way both sides accept an appraisal.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Who Pays' report for three states using public filings. Email 10 state consumer advocate offices and 20 county planning departments. Offer a $12k pilot impact statement on one live docket. Approach two mid-size developers who are stuck in a zoning fight.

title: Wind Tunnel for Agent Markets and Pricing Collusion
one_liner: Simulate your pricing or buying agent against thousands of rival agents to see whether it drifts into tacit collusion, manipulation or first-offer traps before regulators or rivals do.
customer: Revenue-management and pricing-software vendors (hotels, multifamily, retail, insurance), marketplaces running agent-facing APIs, and the antitrust and compliance counsel who advise them. Regulators are a later customer.
problem: Academic work shows LLM pricing agents can converge on supracompetitive prices without communicating. Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace found agent buyers show strong first-proposal bias (a 10-30x advantage for response speed) and can be manipulated. Algorithmic pricing is already drawing antitrust suits and state laws, and nobody has a standard way to show a deployed pricing agent behaves competitively.
solution: Adapt the open-source Magentic Marketplace environment into a test harness with calibrated rival populations (LLM and RL agents). Run repeated-game tests measuring markups against a competitive baseline, information-leakage tests, and manipulation and first-offer sensitivity. Deliver an algorithmic pricing conduct report plus guardrails (randomization, no shared non-public data, price-parity limits) and re-test when the underlying model changes.
why_now: Agentic repricing is spreading, algorithmic-pricing enforcement is active, the simulation environment was open-sourced in late 2025, and models change every quarter so one-off audits go stale.
revenue_model: $40-$150k per audit, $5-$15k/month re-test subscriptions, and law-firm seat licenses.
non_obvious_insight: You cannot inspect intent inside a model, but you can test behavior in a sandbox economy. Like crash tests for cars, a standardized, reproducible test gives defendants a documented duty-of-care defense and gives regulators a common yardstick.
first_30_days: Adapt Magentic Marketplace to a hospitality-pricing scenario and write a methodology note. Approach 3 antitrust boutiques and 3 revenue-management vendors, and sell a $25k pilot audit.

title: Quibi for Home-Care Aides: Serialized Compliance Training
one_liner: Quibi's 90-second premium episodes failed as a consumer subscription; as a serialized vertical drama that home-care aides watch to fulfill their mandatory annual training hours, the same format has a captive, budgeted buyer.
customer: Owners and training directors of home-health and home-care agencies with 20-500 aides. Medicare-certified home health agencies must give each aide annual in-service training (12 hours under federal rules), and many states add annual hours for personal-care aides.
problem: Caregiver turnover benchmarks around 75% in 2025. Required training is slide decks and quizzes that workers click through on phones, yet client falls, infections, abuse-reporting failures and survey citations trace back to it. Agencies pay for training that neither sticks nor improves retention.
solution: A private serialized story of two aides and a difficult client. Each 90-second vertical episode ends on a decision (dementia sundowning, family conflict, suspected neglect); the answer unlocks the next episode. Delivered by SMS or WhatsApp link with no app, in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Haitian Creole. An RN advisor approves content, quiz logs map to training-hour documentation, and supervisors get a completion dashboard. AI-assisted production plus human voice actors keeps a season at low tens of thousands of dollars.
why_now: Microdrama apps are booming: industry trackers put short-drama in-app revenue near $3B in 2025 and forecasts of roughly $8B in 2026, so the habit and format exist. Reported AI-assisted production budgets of $15-80k per series are far below traditional costs. Home-care demand is surging while the workforce shrinks.
revenue_model: $6-10 per aide per month with a $300/mo agency minimum, annual contracts; bespoke episodes on an agency's own policies at $3-5k each; same engine later sold to nursing homes, restaurants and hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Quibi's format was fine and its buyer was wrong. Consumers would not pay $8/mo for premium clips, but mandatory compliance budgets are captive and the outcomes (completion, quiz retention, incident reports, quits) are measurable. Frontline workers already binge microdramas on the same phones, so the drama does the engagement work and the compliance layer does the billing.
first_30_days: Write 6 episodes on three topics (dementia behaviors, fall prevention, abuse reporting) with an RN advisor and produce them for under $5k. Pitch 30 agencies through state home-care association lists and LinkedIn. Run free 30-day pilots at 3 agencies, comparing completion and quiz scores against their current slides, then convert to $500/mo contracts.

title: Safety Compliance-as-a-Service for Robot Deployments
one_liner: A standing team plus software that produces the risk assessments, safety validation and insurer paperwork every facility needs before deploying AMRs, cobots or humanoid pilots.
customer: EHS and operations directors at mid-size 3PLs, manufacturers and food or cold-storage plants, integrators without in-house safety staff, and insurers who want documentation.
problem: Deployments stall at safety sign-off. ISO 10218 was revised in 2025, standards for dynamically stable robots and humanoids are still being written, integrators are overloaded, and insurers and OSHA ask for documented assessments. Amazon's 1M-robot scale keeps injury scrutiny high.
solution: Field engineers plus templated software: site scan, risk assessment against current standards, laser-scanner zone and e-stop validation, speed-and-separation testing, training records and incident logs, with annual recertification. Offer a premium 'humanoid pilot safety case' product.
why_now: Humanoid pilots are moving into real facilities in 2026 (Figure reports about 350 units delivered, Agility has a $300M+ single-customer order) while standards lag. Insurers are starting to require paperwork, so it is a channel as well as a service.
revenue_model: $8-25k per site assessment, $3-8k a year for recertification, and software seats for integrators.
non_obvious_insight: For many humanoid and AMR pilots the true bottleneck is one safety officer's signature, and almost no independent practitioners exist. Insurers will steer clients to whoever produces accepted documentation, which gives you distribution.
first_30_days: Recruit a certified functional-safety engineer as cofounder and build assessment templates. Sell 3 fixed-price assessments at about $10k each from integrators' backlogs, and publish a free humanoid pilot safety checklist to generate inbound.

title: Age Assurance Kit for Small Game Communities
one_liner: A drop-in age-gating kit that never stores IDs, with regulator-ready audit trails, for indie multiplayer studios, mod sites, fan forums and Minecraft-style server networks.
customer: Indie multiplayer studios (5-100 staff) with in-game chat, modding and fan-wiki sites, forums, and server networks selling ranks, mainly in the UK and EU.
problem: The UK Online Safety Act enforcement deadline was 2025-07-25, and Discord announced mandatory face-scan or ID checks worldwide in March 2026. Discord's Sept 2025 breach was claimed to have exposed 2.1M ID photos, and photo checks were beaten with Death Stranding character images. Small operators have mandates with no compliance budget.
solution: An SDK and plugin set (Unity, Unreal, Discord bot, Discourse, WordPress, Minecraft servers) that routes each user through the cheapest sufficient method (on-device estimation, card check, reusable wallet attestations). It stores only a signed over-13 or over-18 token, and ships risk-assessment templates and audit logs.
why_now: Enforcement is live, the Roblox and Discord rollouts set user expectations, and a leaked-ID breach makes 'we never hold your ID' a selling point.
revenue_model: $29-199 per month per community plus $0.02-0.10 per verification, with a documentation package for regulators.
non_obvious_insight: Large vendors sell to big platforms, but the long tail needs self-serve pricing and paperwork, not just a verification call. The liability is holding the ID, so a token-only design is the product, not a feature.
first_30_days: Ship a Discord bot and WordPress plugin on top of an existing estimation and wallet vendor. Recruit 20 forum and server operators through modding and Minecraft communities. Convert 5 to paid plans and write the regulator documentation pack.

title: Peak-Season Exchange for Idle Warehouse Robot Hours
one_liner: A marketplace and price index that moves idle AMRs and robots-as-a-service capacity between 3PLs and retailers to cover seasonal peaks, priced per robot-hour.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs and retailers needing Q4 peak capacity, and owners of idle fleets (integrators, RaaS providers, seasonal retailers, lenders holding repossessed units). Lenders and investors buy the index.
problem: Peaks force 3PLs into premium temp labor, while fleets sized for average load sit idle for half the year at seasonal operators. There is no market price for a robot-hour, so lenders cannot value the assets either.
solution: Standardize robot-hour listings (AMR class, payload, WMS integration) with a 48-hour commissioning kit (mapping, WMS connector) and escrowed insurance. Seed supply from idle demo pools and seasonal owners, and publish a weekly Robot Rate Index by class and region. Add forward contracts for peak later.
why_now: Robot pricing is becoming public and recurring (Figure's planned $600 a month lease, 1X at $499 a month, Agility's $300M+ order), and buyers want outcome pricing and 48-hour product-mix changes. Peak season 2026 is starting now, so the first rentals can be tested against real labor premiums.
revenue_model: 12-18% take rate on rentals, a commissioning fee per deployment, and $10-30k a year for index and benchmark subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Robots are sold as capex but bought as capacity. Once tens of thousands of units exist, capacity will trade like trailers and rail cars, and whoever runs the exchange sets the price benchmark (DAT, Drewry) and owns residual-value data.
first_30_days: Source about 50 idle AMRs from 2 integrators' demo pools and 2 seasonal retailers. Sell 3 emergency Q4 peak rentals to 3PLs paying temp-labor premiums, and publish Robot Rate Index v0 from about 40 collected quotes.

title: Contingency Royalty Audits for Game Developers
one_liner: A $99 automated statement check that finds provable underpayments in publisher royalty reports, then hands winnable cases to forensic accountants on contingency.
customer: Developers signed with publishers who are unrecouped or getting opaque quarterly statements. They pay $99-299 for the check and 20-25% of any recovered money. Referral fees also come from games lawyers and auditors.
problem: Audit clauses exist in most publishing deals (one analysis found them in 88% of deals with an advance), but a formal audit costs more than a small studio can recover, so publishers effectively face none. One 30-contract analysis found 42% gave the publisher 100% of revenue until recoupment. Marketing 'recoupables', vague net-revenue definitions, cross-collateralization and FX and VAT handling all hide errors. Devs sit on a spreadsheet they can't verify.
solution: Devs upload the contract and statements. We rebuild the recoup waterfall from the contract's own definitions and compare it with independent signals: review-count unit estimates, price history and regional mix. We flag anomalies such as marketing above a cap, taxes deducted twice, giveaway keys counted as spend, and FX gaps. A clause pack and a negotiation script push new deals toward Steamworks read-only financial permission for the dev. Flagged cases go to a panel of forensic accountants who send a formal audit notice.
why_now: The 2023-25 layoffs pushed thousands of devs into 'marketing-only' publishing deals with recoup terms. LLMs can now parse contracts and statements at near-zero marginal cost. Funding is tight, so every unpaid royalty matters.
revenue_model: Flat pre-audit fee, 20-25% contingency on recoveries (cheaper than the roughly 40% litigation contingency), and referral fees from lawyers. Later: a paid tier for funds and lenders that want portfolio royalty monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Detection was never the bottleneck. Cost was. A cheap pre-audit that separates provable errors from noise lets an auditor take only winnable cases. Publishers in a small, gossipy industry often settle quickly once a credible notice lands, because they don't want the precedent to spread, and many errors are honest spreadsheet mistakes.
first_30_days: Launch a free recoup-waterfall calculator and a 'publisher-deal red-flag scan' on r/gamedev and dev Discords. Collect about 100 anonymized statements as training and proof data. Sign referral deals with two games-industry lawyers and one forensic accountant. Take the first 5 contingency cases with flagged anomalies over $10k.

title: Listing Bodyguard: Scam-Listing Takedown for Property Managers
one_liner: Continuously scans the web for scam copies of a property manager's listings and takes them down, and gives real prospects a fast way to verify that a listing is legitimate.
customer: Property managers and leasing companies with 100 to 3,000 units, paying a monthly subscription. The buyer is the marketing or leasing director. Secondary buyers are apartment associations, large landlords' insurers and rental listing portals.
problem: Scammers copy a manager's real listing photos, undercut the rent by 25 to 40% and collect application fees and deposits from victims who never see the unit. Victims then show up at the property or call the leasing office furious, and often leave one-star reviews of the real manager. Real leads are poached by the fake listing, and the leasing team wastes hours on angry callers and manual takedown requests to Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace and others. There is no owner of the problem: the listing platforms are slow, police shrug and the PM's syndication vendor does not monitor. AI now makes it trivial to generate thousands of fake listings, with photos rewritten and descriptions localized.
solution: Pull each PM's live listing feed (from the syndication export in AppFolio, Buildium, Yardi or RentManager), compute perceptual hashes of every photo and fingerprints of the description text and address, then continuously search for matches across Craigslist, Zillow-family sites, Facebook (through allowed methods and user reports), OfferUp and the open web through reverse-image APIs. When a match appears on a listing whose contact does not belong to the PM, the system files takedown requests through each platform's copyright, fraud or impersonation channel with evidence, tracks status, and escalates. Prevention layer: every real listing gets a short verification code ('Verify: text 4471 to our verified line'), and a landing page confirms the unit and the real contact, giving prospects a free way to check before wiring money. Weekly reports show scams blocked, leads protected and estimated victim exposure.
why_now: Generative AI made scam listings cheap and scalable in 2025 and 2026, and consumer-protection agencies continue to list rental scams among the top fraud categories. Rental portals are under pressure to verify but are slow. The reverse-image and vision APIs from major providers make similarity search inexpensive, and the takedown channels are already documented, so a small team can automate a job that leasing staff currently do by hand.
revenue_model: $0.50 to $1.50 per active listing per month with a $199 monthly minimum, or a flat tier for portfolios. Upsell: white-label verification pages and analytics for apartment associations, and API licensing to listing portals and insurers who want fewer fraud claims.
non_obvious_insight: To a leasing office, a scam listing is not a consumer-fraud story. It is a top-of-funnel leak and a brand problem, because the scammer steals real leads and the victims blame the PM. Managers already know this but treat it as a nuisance, so there is a budget for a fix but no product. The real moat is the takedown playbook per platform: which channel, which wording, which contact person actually gets a listing removed within hours rather than days.
first_30_days: Manually audit 3 to 5 friendly PMs: take their public listings, run reverse-image searches and show them the scam copies already live (there will be some). That audit is the sales pitch, and most PMs have never looked. Build a script using Google Vision web-detection or TinEye plus Craigslist and Marketplace searches for a first pass, and a shared dashboard for takedown status. Charge $199 per month per portfolio starting in month 2. Ask each PM for a testimonial and a 'stopped 14 scams last quarter' number to bring to the next landlord association talk.

title: Provably Anonymous, Provably Employee Whistleblower Channel
one_liner: A reporting channel where a worker proves they hold a company email using zero-knowledge proofs, without the employer or vendor ever learning who they are.
customer: EU and UK employers with 50-500 staff that must run internal reporting channels, employment-law and compliance firms that deploy them, and works councils.
problem: Whistleblower-directive compliance is often a checkbox. Employees do not believe 'anonymous' hotlines that log IPs and identities, so use is low. Employers get junk or spoofed reports and cannot confirm that a reporter is a real current employee.
solution: ZK-email proofs of an employer-domain, DKIM-signed message let a reporter prove employment without revealing which mailbox. Per-report nullifiers block duplicates, and no identity is stored. Add anonymous two-way messaging, evidence upload, and a 'verified current employee in a group of at least 10' signal to the company. Independent cryptographic review is published.
why_now: ZK-email tooling is open source and maturing, EU digital-identity wallets are due by end 2026, and deepfake and spoofed reports are increasing. Whistleblower rules now apply to smaller firms, so many companies are buying cheap channels for the first time.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,500 per month per company, with a 30% channel margin for law firms and a free tier for firms under 50 staff.
non_obvious_insight: Hotline usage is limited by trust in anonymity, which promises cannot improve, only making identification cryptographically impossible can. The same proof gives employers what they want (verified employee) and gives hostile insiders nothing.
first_30_days: Prototype with open-source zk-email libraries. Line up three employment-law firms and 10 SMEs for a free pilot, and commission a small third-party cryptography review to publish.

title: Callback Verification Network for Invoice-Paying Agents
one_liner: A consortium ledger of verified vendor bank details plus automated out-of-band callbacks that gives accounts-payable agents a signed safe-to-pay attestation before they send money to changed payment instructions.
customer: Bookkeeping and AP-outsourcing firms (each managing 100-300 SMB clients) and AP-automation vendors first, then mid-market controllers ($50M-$1B revenue).
problem: Business email compromise costs roughly $2.8B a year in reported US losses. Humans used to catch odd bank-detail changes by accident, but an AP agent that reads emails and PDFs will follow an instruction injected into an invoice at machine speed (prompt injection maps to 6 of 10 OWASP agentic risks). The US has no Confirmation of Payee, unlike the UK (since 2020) and the EU (Verification of Payee mandated from October 2025).
solution: An API the AP agent calls whenever bank details are new or changed. We match against a shared ledger of callback-verified details contributed by all customers, run TIN and account-ownership checks, and if still unverified place an outbound voice-agent call to the number on file from the last verified contract or W-9, never the number on the invoice. We return a signed attestation that the payment policy requires, and anything unattested routes to a human. An optional guarantee covers attested payments.
why_now: Agentic AP is shipping in 2026, Nacha's 2026 fraud-monitoring rule phases push originators to prove controls, Google's threat group documents autonomous multi-agent credential harvesting in under 6 hours, and voice agents make a verification callback cost cents instead of a clerk's ten minutes.
revenue_model: $3-8 per new-or-changed-details verification, $0.15-0.40 per payment monitored, and a guarantee premium (about 1-3 bps of attested payment value) once loss data exists.
non_obvious_insight: Agents remove the accidental friction that used to stop fraud, so the defense that works is a channel the attacker and any injected prompt cannot touch. A shared ledger strengthens with every adopter, which builds Confirmation of Payee bottom-up in a country whose banks will not build it.
first_30_days: Sign 10 bookkeeping firms that together manage 1,000+ SMB vendors. Run callbacks semi-manually with a voice agent and humans on escalation, and sell a verified-vendor book at $99 per month per client. Wire a webhook into one AP tool (Bill.com or Ramp style) so the attestation gates payment approval.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Dead Importers
one_liner: A contingency service that finds failed or dormant importers whose IEEPA refund claims are stranded, revives them or works through their bankruptcy trustee, and files the claims through a licensed broker.
customer: Chapter 7 trustees and ABC assignees of failed importers, plus founders of dissolved or dormant small importers. They pay 20-30% of recovered dollars. Secondary customers are claim buyers who want vetted entry-level claim files.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP is now refunding through CAPE in phases: Phase 1 opened Apr 20 for unliquidated and recently liquidated entries, Phase 2 came in June, and Phase 3 (late July) covers finally liquidated entries only for importers who sued at the CIT. Refunds go to the importer of record (or the broker who filed the entry). Every entry has its own clock, including the 180-day protest window. A large tail of small importers closed or went dark during the 2025 tariff shock. Their refunds are six-figure receivables spread across hundreds of ACE entries. They appear on nobody's balance sheet, and nobody at the dead company is watching for them. A trustee liquidating the estate usually does not know the asset exists.
solution: Build an entry-level refund estimator from public bill-of-lading data, HTS lines, country of origin and the IEEPA rate schedule. Cross-match importer names against state dissolution lists and PACER filings to rank stranded claims by likely dollar value. Then run the recovery: (1) approach trustees with an asset-discovery letter and a court-approvable contingency engagement; (2) for dissolved entities, reinstate the corporation under state law, re-enroll ACH, and file CF-4811 designations where needed; (3) have a licensed broker file CAPE declarations for the entries that broker filed; (4) send finally liquidated entries to partner trade counsel for CIT reliquidation orders under the July 17 order. The moat is a licensed-broker partner plus a pipeline of claims that nobody else is hunting.
why_now: IEEPA was struck down Feb 20, 2026. CAPE phases rolled out Apr-Jul 2026, and the July 17 CIT order created a court-driven Phase 3. Per-entry deadlines are now running. Existing refund tools (deadline trackers and CAPE filing helpers) all sell to living importers who are already paying attention. Nobody productized the orphaned-claim hunt.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on refunds recovered, plus interest. Trustee engagements are approved by the bankruptcy court as contingency fee arrangements. A secondary line sells diligenced claim packages to claim buyers at a flat fee per package.
non_obvious_insight: The refund is attached to the importer-of-record number, not to whoever was actually hurt, and only the IOR or the filing broker can claim it in the early phases. Brokers hold the entry data but their powers of attorney die with the client, and chasing a dead client is unbillable work, so nobody does it. A broker can still file CAPE for entries it filed, which makes the broker the key that unlocks these claims. Outsiders see the refund as a tax-accounting topic. Insiders see it as an unclaimed-property hunt across ACE.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 2025 importer-level volumes for China, Vietnam, India and other tariffed origins from ImportYeti or a cheap paid BOL feed, then estimate each importer's IEEPA duty. Week 2: cross-match against CA, NY, TX, FL and NJ dissolution records and PACER chapter 7 and ABC filings, and rank the top 150 targets above about $50k. Week 3: send trustees a one-page asset-discovery letter, since trustee contact info is public, and have a trade lawyer draft the contingency engagement. Week 4: sign the first 3-5 estates, or dormant founders, and file the first CAPE declarations through the partner broker.
